title: Missing Number
summary: Figure-based puzzles — paired grids, single grids, circles — where one cell is hidden behind a numerical rule. Every rule connects the cells of a row (or segment), and the same rule is demonstrated by at least two complete instances. The winning habit is two-line verification: fit the rule on one complete row, confirm on the other, then apply. Digit-sum and digit-reversal variants reward students who switch families quickly when plain arithmetic stalls.

subtopics.title: How missing-number puzzles work
subtopics.concept:
A figure — two square grids, or concentric circles, or a triangle of numbers — carries a **hidden rule** connecting its cells. One cell is replaced by '?'. Your job is to extract the rule from the *complete* instances and apply it once.

The examiner's design guarantees the rule: the same relationship must hold in **every** complete row/segment. So the method is mechanical:

1. **Read two complete rows** (or segments) side by side.
2. **Test simple candidates** in order: sum, difference, product, 'multiply then add/subtract a constant', square, digit-sum. CGL rules are almost always one of these.
3. **Confirm the candidate on the second complete row.** A rule that works on one row but not the other is wrong — this single check eliminates nearly every error.
4. Apply the confirmed rule to the incomplete row.

Speed note: start from the biggest number in the row and ask 'how do the other two build it?' — most rules build the largest cell from the smaller ones.

formulas.name: Rule confirmation
formulas.note: Two agreeing instances pin the rule; one instance pins nothing.

formulas.name: Common families
formulas.tex: a+b,\ a-b,\ a \times b,\ ab \pm k,\ (a \pm b)k,\ a^2 \pm b,\ \text{digitsum}
formulas.note: Test sums/products first — they cover ~80% of CGL puzzles.

tricks.title: Two-row confirmation
tricks.body: Never answer from one fitted row. Write the candidate rule symbolically ('c = a×b + 1'), check it on the second complete row, then apply. Ten seconds of checking prevents the most common wrong answer in this topic — a rule that fits only the first row.

example.solution: Guess → confirm on the spare row → apply. In that order, every time.

mistakes: Fitting a rule to the first row only and answering immediately.
Assuming left-to-right reading of the figure when the rule runs along columns or diagonals.
Over-complicated rules (three operations) when a simple one fits both rows.
subtopics.notes:
### One hidden rule, found by systematic guessing

A figure — grids, circles, triangles — carries a hidden rule connecting its numbers; one cell is missing. You are not looking for THE rule, only for A simple rule that fits every complete row/segment and gives one of the options.

**The standard search order.** For each complete row (or matching pair of cells), test in this sequence and stop at the first rule that fits everywhere:
1. Sums and differences: third = first + second, or their difference.
2. Products and quotients: third = first × second (watch a constant ×, like 2ab).
3. Squares and near-squares: third = a², a² + b, a² + b², a² − 1 — numbers like 25, 26, 48, 49 are square magnets.
4. Mixed: first² ± second, (first + second)², first × second ± constant.

**Fit everywhere, not somewhere.** A rule that works on one row is a coincidence. Every complete row must reproduce its third number (and every complete grid must reproduce the other grid's numbers) before you trust it on the missing cell. Two rows fitting 'a + b' while the third fits 'a × b' means the rule is wrong — real exam rules are uniform.

**Two-grid puzzles.** When two complete grids sit beside an incomplete one, the rule lives *inside* each grid (usually row by row), and the second grid simply repeats the first grid's rule with different numbers. Solve grid 1 completely first, verify on grid 2, then apply to grid 3.

**Segments (circles, triangles).** Match positions: opposite segments, or corner-vs-centre. Common segment rules: opposite pairs share a constant sum; centre = sum (or product) of corners; each ring adds a constant.

**Option-driven pruning.** If the missing cell must be, say, odd, every even option dies — check parity first. If rows are increasing, a decreasing option dies. Prune before deep work; with two options left, often only one fits a plausible rule.

**Anchor on the biggest number.** The largest cell of a row is almost always the output. Try to rebuild it from the smaller cells: 26 from 5 and 1 (5² + 1), 21 from 4 and 5 (4 × 5 + 1). Reading left to right hides the rule; rebuilding the largest cell exposes it.

**Size tells you the operation.** Compare the output with the inputs: output ≈ sum → addition family; output ≈ product → multiplication family; output ≈ first² → square family; output smaller than both → difference, average or a digit rule. One glance at the size cuts the search list in half.

**Why distractors look right.** Exam setters plant the value of the *most tempting wrong rule* in the options: the bare product when the rule is product + 1, the plain square when it is square − 1, the unreversed sum when the rule reverses. If your answer equals a 'simpler' version of the rule, re-check that the simpler rule really fails a complete row.

### Quick revision
- Test rules in order: + / − → × / ÷ → squares → mixed (a² ± b, (a+b)²...).
- The rule must fit EVERY complete row/segment — one fit is a coincidence.
- Two grids: solve grid 1, verify on grid 2, apply to grid 3.
- Segments: match opposite positions; centre often = sum/product of corners.
- Prune by parity and trend before hunting the rule.

patterns.name: Third number from two: linear rules
patterns.howToSpot: Rows of two/three numbers where the third is a plain sum, difference or multiple of the first.
patterns.logic:
1. Test c = ka (constant multiple) and c = a ± b.
2. k must be the same in every row.
3. Apply to the incomplete row.

*Why it works:* the simplest rules are linear, so they are tried first.

patterns.name: Square-based rules
patterns.logic:
1. Test c = a² ± b, c = a² ± 1, c = a² + b².
2. Square the first number and see what the leftover equals.
3. Verify on all rows before answering.

*Why it works:* squares plus a small correction are a favourite exam construction.

patterns.name: Two-grid analogy
patterns.howToSpot: Two complete grids and a third with a missing cell.
patterns.logic:
1. Find grid 1's row rule.
2. Verify it reproduces grid 2 exactly.
3. Apply it to grid 3's incomplete row.

*Why it works:* the second grid is a free verification of the rule.

patterns.name: Verify-then-answer discipline
patterns.howToSpot: Any figure where several rules 'almost' fit, or a cross/2×2 layout.
patterns.logic:
1. Candidate rule must fit every complete row/segment AND match an option.
2. For 2×2 crosses: test diagonal products and sums too.
3. Reject a rule that fits two rows but fails the third.

*Why it works:* exam figures are built from one uniform rule; near-misses are bait.

example.solution: Both rows square the first number → 15² = **225**.

subtopics.title: Grids with row (or column) rules
subtopics.concept:
The classic CGL format: **two complete 3×3 grids and a third with one missing cell** — or a single grid whose rows share a rule. The rule runs row-wise ('in each row, third number = first × second + 1') or column-wise ('third column = first + second'); the reading direction does not matter to the method — a column rule on a grid is a row rule on its transposed rows.

**Attack order** for two-grid puzzles: compare the *first rows* of both grids, then the *second rows*. Whichever pair shares a clean rule gives you f. For single grids, the two complete rows act as the two instances.

Typical CGL rules, with a worked instance each:

- $c = a \times b + k$: 3, 4, 13 and 5, 2, 11 (k = 1)
- $c = (a + b) \times k$: 4, 7, 22 and 6, 3, 18 (k = 2)
- $c = a \times (b - 1)$: 6, 3, 15 and 8, 4, 28
- $c = a^2 - b$: 8, 15, 49 and 7, 10, 39
- $c = (a + b) \div 2$: 12, 8, 10 and 20, 6, 13

tricks.title: Anchor on the largest cell
tricks.body: Write the largest cell of a row first and rebuild it: 22 = (4 + 7) × 2, 49 = 8² − 15, 13 = 26 ÷ 2. Building the largest from the rest exposes the rule faster than scanning left to right.

example.solution: Largest cell = output; smaller cells = inputs. Almost always true in CGL.

tricks.title: Transcribe the figure as rows
tricks.body: Copy the grid into your rough column as three horizontal rows, question mark included. Reading values off the figure mid-calculation is where transposition errors come from.

example.solution: A three-line transcription beats squinting at the figure.

mistakes: Mixing up the two grids — applying grid 1's row to grid 2's columns.
Choosing between two half-fitting rules by feel instead of testing both fully.
subtopics.notes:
### The CGL workhorse: grids where rows (or columns) share a rule

The format: a 3×3 grid — sometimes two complete grids and a third with a hole. Each row obeys the same rule turning its first two numbers into its third. Everything is row-arithmetic; the skill is finding the rule fast.

**The two-number bridge.** Cover the third column and hunt a bridge from column 1 to column 2 — or from columns 1+2 to column 3. The classic bridges, in testing order:
- $c = a + b$ and $c = a - b$ (or $|a-b|$) — check signs.
- $c = a \times b$; then $c = 2ab$, $c = ab + k$, $c = ab - k$ with a small constant.
- $c = a^2 + b$, $c = b^2 + a$, $c = a^2 + b^2$ — the Pythagorean look (3-4-25, 5-12-169).
- $c = (a + b)^2$ or $(a - b)^2$ — results like 49, 64, 144 are squares.
- Digit tricks (see the digit-operations lesson): digit sums and reversals.

**Confirm on every row.** Compute the candidate rule on all complete rows. A rule fitting row 1 and row 3 but not row 2 is dead — keep hunting. This one habit separates solvers from guessers.

**Column rules.** When rows refuse every bridge, the rule runs down the columns: third row = f(first row, second row) cell by cell, or column 2 = average of columns 1 and 3, or column 3 = column 1 − column 2. Same procedure, transposed.

**Two complete grids.** Solve the left grid's rule first (it has no hole), verify it reproduces the middle grid, then apply to the right one. The rule never changes between grids; only the numbers do.

**Circle and triangle figures.** Match by position: opposite segments of a circle (constant sum or product), corners vs centre of a triangle (centre = sum or product of corners), inner ring vs outer ring. Write the matched pairs as little equations and look for the common thread.

**Worked walk-through.** Rows (4, 6, 10), (5, 3, 22), (7, 2, ?). Sum: 4 + 6 = 10 ✓ on row 1 — tempting — but 5 + 3 = 8 ✗ on row 2, so the sum rule dies. Product: 24 ✗. Square family: $a^2 - b$ gives 16 − 6 = 10 ✓ and 25 − 3 = 22 ✓. Only now apply it: 49 − 2 = **47**. Notice the trap: had you stopped at row 1, you would have answered 7 + 2 = 9. The discipline is the same every time: one candidate, all rows, next candidate.

**Speed tricks.** Keep squares to 25 and cubes to 12 memorised; spot $a^2 - b^2 = (a+b)(a-b)$ to avoid big squaring; and when third cells are all odd while inputs are mixed parity, product ± 1 is a strong suspect.

### Quick revision
- Bridge hunt order: + / − → × / ÷ → ×2, ab ± k → a²+b, b²+a, a²+b² → (a±b)².
- The rule must reproduce EVERY complete row (and grid 2 in two-grid puzzles).
- Rows stuck → test columns; grids stuck → test opposite segments / centre vs corners.
- Squares in the options (25, 49, 144) beg for a square-based rule.
- Digit sums and reversals are fair game — see digit-operations.

patterns.name: Row sums and differences
patterns.howToSpot: Third column close to the sum or difference of the first two.
patterns.logic:
1. Test c = a + b on all rows; then c = |a − b|.
2. Watch sign traps (a − b vs b − a).
3. Apply the fitting rule to the incomplete row.

*Why it works:* the default construction of exam grids.

example.solution: c = a + b fits every row → 7 + 11 = **18**.

patterns.name: Products, doubled products and squares
patterns.howToSpot: Third column much larger than the first two, or a perfect square.
patterns.logic:
1. Test c = ab, then 2ab, then ab ± k.
2. If c is a square, test a² + b² and (a+b)².
3. Fit all rows.

*Why it works:* multiplicative and square rules create the 'too big' signature.

patterns.name: Column rules
patterns.howToSpot: Rows refuse every bridge; try the grid vertically.
patterns.logic:
1. Test column3 = column1 ± column2 (cell by cell down the rows).
2. Test column2 = (column1 + column3) / 2.
3. Confirm on every complete column.

*Why it works:* transposing the rule is the standard disguise.

patterns.name: Circle and triangle segments
patterns.howToSpot: Numbers around a circle or in triangle corners with a centre.
patterns.logic:
1. Pair opposite segments; test constant sum, then product.
2. For triangles: centre vs sum/product of corners.
3. Verify on every matched pair.

*Why it works:* segment figures repeat one relation across matched positions.

subtopics.title: Digit-sum and digit-reversal rules
subtopics.concept:
A chunk of CGL missing-number puzzles operate on **digits**, not values:

- **Digit-sum rule**: $c = \text{digitsum}(a) + \text{digitsum}(b) \pm k$, e.g. 28, 9, 21 since 10 + 9 + 2 = 21 and 36, 23, 16 since 9 + 5 + 2 = 16.
- **Reversal rule**: $c = \text{reverse}(a + b)$, e.g. 43 + 14 = 57 → **75**; 34 + 43 = 77 → 77.

These look alien at first glance precisely because the *values* don't line up — that mismatch is the tell. If neither sums, products, nor squares fit the two complete rows, test digit operations before anything exotic.

Digit-sum speed: add digits in pairs, and remember a number and its digit-sum are equal mod 9 — so digit-sum questions never need long addition.

tricks.title: The mismatch trigger
tricks.body: If 30 seconds of standard rules fails on both rows, immediately test: (i) digit sums, (ii) reversed sum, (iii) product of digit sums. One of these fits in the large majority of 'stuck' puzzles.

example.solution: Standard rules fail → digit operations, tested with the same two-row confirmation.

tricks.title: Reversal sanity check
tricks.body: A reversed-digit answer must read backwards cleanly: reverse(57) = 75. If the sum ends in 0 the reversal is not defined for CGL purposes — such puzzles avoid those sums, so if your sum ends in 0 you have the wrong rule.

example.solution: Sum first, then flip the two digits — a two-step rule, confirmed on two rows.

mistakes: Reversing the inputs instead of the sum (43 → 34) when the rule reverses the result.
Digit-sum slips on numbers containing 0 or repeated digits.
Abandoning the two-instance confirmation because the rule 'looks digital' — confirm it anyway.
subtopics.notes:
### When the rule lives inside the digits

A large family of missing-number puzzles never add the *values* — they operate on **digits**: sums of digits, reversed digits, products of digits. Recognising the family early saves minutes.

**The digit-sum rule.** $S(n)$ = sum of a number's digits: $S(47) = 11$. Typical rules:
- third = $S(a) + S(b)$ — e.g. 47 and 38 give $11 + 11 = 22$;
- third = $S(a + b)$ — add first, then sum digits (68 → 14);
- third = $2 \times S(a)$ — doubling a digit sum.
Tell them apart by testing one complete row with each variant; only one will fit both rows.

**The reversal family.** $R(n)$ = the number with digits reversed: $R(43) = 34$. Common rules:
- third = $R(a) + R(b)$ — the classic 'reversed-sum' grid (34 + 41 = 75);
- third = $|R(a) - b|$;
- third = $R(a + b)$ — add first, then flip (39 → 93).
Reversal rules produce third numbers whose digits are the 'mirror image' of the row's story — options like 75 next to 43 and 14 are a waving flag.

**The digit-product rule.** $P(n)$ = product of digits: $P(47) = 28$. Rules: third = $P(a)$, third = $P(a) + P(b)$, third = $P(a) \times S(b)$. Zero is the instant tell — a row containing 0 or 10 has digit product 0, which usually kills product rules on sight.

**Spotting the family.** Hints that the rule is digit-based:
- The third numbers are far too small or too large for plain sums/products of the values.
- Options cluster near digit-scale numbers (5-30) while the values are two-digit.
- The same digits recur across rows (43/34, 62/26) — reversal is in play.

**Verification is cheap here.** Digit rules are one line of arithmetic per row — check all complete rows, not just one. And compute the final answer with the SAME variant that fit, not with the variant you tried first.

**The mod-9 shortcut.** A number and its digit sum leave the same remainder on division by 9. So if a digit-sum rule is in play, the output and the inputs' digit sums must agree mod 9 — a quick way to kill an option without computing every digit sum. Example: S(47) + S(38) = 22; check 47 + 38 = 85 → 85 and 22 both leave 4 on division by 9 ✓.

**Reversal traps.** Two traps dominate: reversing the *inputs* when the rule reverses the *result* (and vice versa), and sums ending in 0 (R(40) = 04 = 4) — setters avoid them, so a 0-ending sum usually means you picked the wrong variant. Palindromes (77, 66) sitting in the grid are a gift: they are identical under reversal and hint that reversal is part of the rule.

### Quick revision
- $S(n)$ = digit sum (47 → 11); $R(n)$ = reversal (43 → 34); $P(n)$ = digit product (47 → 28).
- Standard rules: $S(a)+S(b)$, $S(a+b)$, $2S(a)$, $R(a)+R(b)$, $|R(a)-b|$, $R(a+b)$, $P(a)+P(b)$.
- Test each variant on a complete row; only one fits all rows.
- Options far smaller than the values → digit rule; mirror-looking pairs → reversal.
- Zeros kill digit-product rules instantly.

patterns.name: Digit-sum rules
patterns.howToSpot: Third numbers are small (5-30) while values are two-digit.
patterns.logic:
1. S(n) = digit sum. Test c = S(a) + S(b), then c = S(a + b).
2. Test on a complete row first, then everywhere.
3. Apply the fitting variant to the missing cell.

*Why it works:* digit sums shrink big numbers into option-sized ones.

patterns.name: Reversal rules
patterns.howToSpot: Digits mirror across the row (43 beside 34); third numbers look like flipped sums.
patterns.logic:
1. R(n) = reversed digits. Test c = R(a) + R(b).
2. Then |R(a) − b| and R(a + b).
3. Check on all rows.

*Why it works:* reversal is the most reused digit trick in CGL grids.

patterns.name: Digit-product rules
patterns.howToSpot: Third numbers too small even for digit sums, or options under ~30.
patterns.logic:
1. P(n) = product of digits. Test c = P(a), then P(a) + P(b).
2. A 0 in the values usually kills product rules — check first.
3. Fit everywhere.

*Why it works:* digit products collapse two-digit numbers into tiny ones.

patterns.name: Mixed digit arithmetic
patterns.howToSpot: Digit sums combined with the other value: multiply, double, or weight.
patterns.logic:
1. Test c = 2·S(a), c = S(a) × b, c = S(a) + b.
2. The b-value stays whole while the digit-sum shrinks a.
3. Verify variant on all rows.

*Why it works:* mixing one digit op with one raw value hides the rule one level deeper.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A 3×3 grid with one missing cell; rows (or columns) share a hidden rule.
pyqPatterns.approach: Test bridges in order: a+b, |a−b|, ab, 2ab, ab±k, a²+b², (a+b)² — fit on every complete row before applying.

example.solution: Plain a+b fails (9, 12). Divide out: 15 = 5×3, 28 = 7×4 — the multipliers 5, 7 are one less than the first numbers → c = (a−1)×b → (9−1)×5 = **40**.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two complete grids and an incomplete third.
pyqPatterns.approach: Derive the rule on the first grid, verify it on the second, then apply to the third.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Output cells sit next to perfect squares (26, 48, 50, 63...).
pyqPatterns.approach: Square the first (or second) input and read the leftover: a² ± b, a² ± 1, a² + b².

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Numbers placed in sectors of a circle or corners of a triangle with a centre value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Treat each sector as a row, or pair opposite sectors; test constant sum, then centre = sum/product of corners.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Mirror-image digits across the row (23 beside 32); outputs look like scrambled sums.
pyqPatterns.approach: Test R(a) + R(b) and R(a + b); confirm on both complete rows.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Outputs are small and factor neatly into the digits of the inputs.
pyqPatterns.approach: P(n) = product of digits; test P(a), P(a) + P(b), then weighted mixtures.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Third numbers tiny compared with the values.
pyqPatterns.approach: S(a)+S(b) first, then S(a+b); fit on all complete rows.

solvedExamples.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 7, 9, 4  **Grid 2:** 8, 5, 7  **Grid 3:** 11, 3, ?

(In each grid, the numbers are read left to right as one row.)
solvedExamples.solution: Test the row rule on both complete grids: 7 + 9 + 4 = 20 and 8 + 5 + 7 = 20 — the **row sum is always 20**. So 11 + 3 + ? = 20 → ? = **6**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Add a complete row; if two complete rows share the same total, the rule is 'sum = constant'.

solvedExamples.solution: Each row: third = first × second. Check: 4×3 = 12 ✓; 5×4 = 20 ✓. So 7 × 2 = **14**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: The largest cell factorises neatly into the other two — test the product rule first.
solvedExamples.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

solvedExamples.solution: Plain sums fail (42 ≠ 24 as a value... but 24 is 42 reversed). Rule: **reverse the digits of (first + second)**. Check: 24+18 = 42 → 24 ✓; 32+13 = 45 → 54 ✓. So 26+15 = 41 → reversed = **14**. (41 is the unreversed sum — the planted trap.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: When sums 'almost' match, check whether the third cell is the reversed sum.

solvedExamples.solution: Digit-sum rule: third = digit-sum(first) + digit-sum(second) + 2. Check: 10 + 9 + 2 = 21 ✓; 9 + 5 + 2 = 16 ✓. So 9 + 8 + 2 = **19**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Sums/products fail → add the digits of each number, then look for the constant.

practice.solution: Rule: third = first × second + 1. Check: 3×4 + 1 = 13 ✓; 5×2 + 1 = 11 ✓. So 6×3 + 1 = **19**. (18 is the bare product — the near-miss trap.)
practice.shortcut: Product first, then look for the small constant: +1 here.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Rule: third = first − second. Check: 9−2 = 7 ✓; 12−5 = 7 ✓. So 15 − 9 = **6**. (7 repeats in the first two rows — do not copy it into the third.)
practice.shortcut: Same answer twice in a row is a coincidence trap; always derive, never pattern-copy.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 22 = (4+7)×2; confirm 18 = (6+3)×2 ✓. Rule: third = (first + second) × 2. So (9+5)×2 = **28**. (45 is 9×5 — the product trap.)
practice.shortcut: Large third cell with modest inputs → try (a+b)×k or a×b first.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.shortcut: When a×b overshoots (30 vs 15), test a×(b−1) or b×(a−1) — the 'one less' family.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Digit sums: 29 → 11, 14 → 5; 11 + 5 = 16 and 18 − 16 = 2. Confirm: 38 → 11, 25 → 7; 11 + 7 + 2 = 20 ✓. Rule: third = digitsum(first) + digitsum(second) + 2. So 11 + 4 + 2 = **17**.
practice.shortcut: Standard rules dead for two seconds → switch to digit sums and find the constant.

practice.solution: 49 = 8² − 15; confirm 39 = 7² − 10 = 49 − 10 ✓. Rule: third = (first)² − second. So 6² − 11 = 36 − 11 = **25**. (36 is 6² without subtracting 11.)
practice.shortcut: The third number sits just below the square of the first (49 is 8² = 64 minus 15), so test a² − b: 6² − 11 = **25**.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 10 = (12+8) ÷ 2; confirm 13 = (20+6) ÷ 2 = 26 ÷ 2 ✓. Rule: third = average of first two. So (14+4) ÷ 2 = **9**. (18 is the un-divided sum.)
practice.shortcut: Third cell sitting between the other two → test their average.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 25 = 5×(6−1); confirm 21 = 7×(4−1) ✓. Rule: third = first × (second − 1). So 9 × (3−1) = **18**. (27 = 9×3 is the bare product.)
practice.shortcut: a×b too big by exactly a (or b) → the second factor carries a −1.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: In each row, third column = first + second: 6+5 = 11 ✓; 9+4 = 13 ✓. So 8 + 7 = **15**. (56 = 8×7 is the product trap.)
practice.shortcut: Column-wise rule — read each row as (a, b, a+b); the check rows confirm instantly.
practice.pattern: column rule in a single grid

practice.q:
Numbers are given in segments of a circular figure, each segment read as (outer, inner, centre):

**15   12   12**

**20   11   36**

**17    9    ?**
practice.solution: 12 = (15−12)×4; confirm 36 = (20−11)×4 = 9×4 ✓. Rule: centre = (outer − inner) × 4. So (17−9)×4 = **32**. (36 repeats the previous centre — a copy trap.)
practice.shortcut: Small centres from big outers → difference × constant is the natural family.

practice.solution: 43 + 14 = 57 → reversed = 75 ✓; 34 + 43 = 77 → reversed = 77 ✓. Rule: third = reverse(first + second). So 26 + 15 = 41 → **14**. (41, 51, 62 are the sum and the reversed inputs — all traps.)
practice.shortcut: Palindrome check row (77 → 77) is the giveaway that reversal is involved.

practice.solution: 31 = 45 − 14 = 9×5 − (9+5); confirm 34 = 48 − 14 = 8×6 − (8+6) ✓. Rule: third = product − sum. So 40 − 14 = **26**. (40 is the bare product.)
practice.shortcut: Constant 14 = a+b in both rows — subtract the sum from the product.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Third = first + second: 4 + 9 = 13 and 7 + 6 = 13. So 5 + 8 = **13**. The repeated 13s tempt you to copy — derive it; the rule happens to give 13 again, but only the derivation proves it. (40 = 5×8 is the product trap.)
practice.shortcut: When every third cell matches, verify the sum rule before trusting a copy.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: 64 = 100 − 36 = 10² − 6²; confirm 128 = 144 − 16 = 12² − 4² ✓. Rule: third = a² − b². So 81 − 25 = **56**. (45 = 9×5 is the product trap; 70 and 85 come from slipping the squares.)
practice.shortcut: Both inputs squaring cleanly and a big third cell → a² − b².
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.shortcut: ab + a + b factorises as (a+1)(b+1) − 1 — a fast mental identity.
practice.pattern: single grid, rows share a rule

practice.solution: Second number = 4 × first: 3 × 4 = 12 ✓, 7 × 4 = 28 ✓. So 9 × 4 = **36**. (27 uses ×3, which fits neither row.)
practice.shortcut: Divide the output by the input — a constant quotient means a constant multiplier.

practice.solution: a + b gives 7 and 7, not 10 and 12 — the first number counts twice. Rule: third = 2 × first + second: 6 + 4 = 10 ✓, 10 + 2 = 12 ✓. So 12 + 5 = **17**. (16 doubles the wrong number.)
practice.shortcut: Output just above a + b by exactly one input → that input is doubled.

practice.solution: Sum and product both fail (9, 20 against 11). Rule: third = 3 × first − second: 15 − 4 = 11 ✓, 18 − 2 = 16 ✓. So 24 − 3 = **21**. (24 forgets to subtract the second number.)
practice.shortcut: Output between a and 3a → try ka ± b.

practice.solution: 10 = 3² + 1 and 37 = 6² + 1. So 8² + 1 = **65**. (64 is the bare square — the near-miss.)
practice.shortcut: Outputs one above a perfect square → a² + 1.

practice.solution: 19 = 4² + 3 and 9 = 2² + 5 — the SECOND number is squared. Rule: third = second² + first. So 5² + 6 = **31**. (41 squares the wrong number: 6² + 5.)
practice.shortcut: Try squaring each input in turn; only one choice fits both rows.

practice.solution: 25 and 36 are perfect squares: 25 = (2 + 3)², 36 = (4 + 2)². Rule: third = (first + second)². So (3 + 5)² = **64**. (34 = 3² + 5² squares separately.)
practice.shortcut: Every output a perfect square → find what is being squared.

practice.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 3, 5, 16  **Grid 2:** 4, 6, 25  **Grid 3:** 5, 7, ?

(Each grid is read left to right as one row.)
practice.solution: Grid 1: 3 × 5 + 1 = 16; grid 2 confirms: 4 × 6 + 1 = 25 ✓. Grid 3: 5 × 7 + 1 = **36**. (35 is the bare product.)
practice.shortcut: Solve grid 1, confirm on grid 2, apply to grid 3.

practice.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 6, 4, 18  **Grid 2:** 5, 7, 30  **Grid 3:** 8, 3, ?

(Each grid is read left to right as one row.)
practice.solution: Products 24 and 35 overshoot by exactly the first number (6 and 5). Rule: third = first × (second − 1): 6 × 3 = 18 ✓, 5 × 6 = 30 ✓. So 8 × 2 = **16**. (21 = 3 × 7 reduces the wrong factor.)
practice.shortcut: Product too big by one input → that input's partner carries a −1.

practice.q:
Study the pattern and find the missing number.

**Grid 1:** 8, 9, 8  **Grid 2:** 12, 6, 7  **Grid 3:** 10, 4, ?

(Each grid is read left to right as one row.)
practice.solution: No clean a-to-c bridge exists, so total the rows: 8 + 9 + 8 = 25 and 12 + 6 + 7 = 25. Every grid sums to 25 → 10 + 4 + ? = 25 → ? = **11**.
practice.shortcut: When bridges fail, add each complete row — equal totals mean a constant-sum rule.

practice.solution: Row 1 tempts with 2 + 4 = 6, but row 2 gives 5 + 3 = 8 ≠ 13 — the sum rule dies. Product − 2 fits both: 8 − 2 = 6 ✓, 15 − 2 = 13 ✓. So 24 − 2 = **22**. (10 is the sum rule that only fitted row 1.)
practice.shortcut: A rule that fits one row is a coincidence until the second row agrees.

practice.solution: Row 1 looks like a product (2 × 4 = 8), but row 2 breaks it (5 × 3 = 15 ≠ 28). Rule: first² + second: 4 + 4 = 8 ✓, 25 + 3 = 28 ✓. So 36 + 2 = **38**. (12 is the product rule; 34 subtracts instead of adding.)
practice.shortcut: Test the second row before trusting the first.

practice.solution: The multipliers differ (×3, then ×6), so no constant multiple fits. 12 = 4² − 4 and 42 = 7² − 7 ✓. So 9² − 9 = **72**. (81 is the bare square; 36 = 9 × 4 copies row 1's ×3 idea.)
practice.shortcut: Changing multiplier equal to (a − 1) → a × (a − 1) = a² − a.

practice.solution: Third = first − second: 15 − 7 = 8 ✓, 20 − 9 = 11 ✓. So 18 − 5 = **13**. (23 adds instead.)
practice.shortcut: Output smaller than the first input → subtraction.

practice.solution: Sums are 14 and 16; the outputs are 11 and 13 — always 3 less. Rule: third = first + second − 3. So 11 − 3 = **8**. (11 is the bare sum; 1 is the difference.)
practice.shortcut: Constant gap between output and a + b → a + b ± k.

practice.solution: Products are 12 and 10; outputs are exactly double. Rule: third = 2 × first × second. So 2 × 24 = **48**. (24 is the undoubled product.)
practice.shortcut: Output ÷ product constant → k × ab.

practice.solution: 5 = 1² + 2² and 29 = 2² + 5² ✓. Rule: third = first² + second². So 9 + 36 = **45**. (81 = (3 + 6)² squares the sum instead.)
practice.shortcut: Output neither sum nor product but beats both → sum of squares.

practice.solution: The missing cell is in the middle, so read each row as (left, middle, right): 9 = (6 + 12) ÷ 2 ✓, 20 = (15 + 25) ÷ 2 ✓. Middle = average of the outer two → (8 + 20) ÷ 2 = **14**. (28 forgets to halve.)
practice.shortcut: A middle cell sitting between its neighbours → average.

practice.solution: Rows resist every bridge (4, 7 → 3 but 5, 2 → 9). Read down the columns instead: 4 + 5 = 9 ✓, 7 + 2 = 9 ✓ — the bottom row is the sum of the two above. So 3 + 9 = **12**. (18 = 9 + 9 is a row-wise guess.)
practice.shortcut: Rows stuck → try columns: bottom = top ± middle, cell by cell.

practice.q: Numbers are written in the six sectors of a circle. Reading opposite sectors as pairs: **14 – 9**, **11 – 12**, **16 – ?**. Find the missing number.
practice.solution: Each opposite pair sums to the same total: 14 + 9 = 23, 11 + 12 = 23. So 16 + ? = 23 → ? = **7**. (9 copies a neighbour; 25 is 16 + 9.)
practice.shortcut: Opposite sectors → constant sum (or product) first.

practice.q:
In each triangle the corners are (left, right, top) and a number sits in the centre:

**(2, 3, 4) → 20**

**(1, 5, 3) → 18**

**(4, 2, 5) → ?**
practice.solution: Product of corners fails (24 ≠ 20), sum fails (9). Rule: centre = (left + right) × top: (2 + 3) × 4 = 20 ✓, (1 + 5) × 3 = 18 ✓. So (4 + 2) × 5 = **30**. (40 is the product of all three corners.)
practice.shortcut: Centre just below the corner product → try (x + y) × z.

practice.solution: Outputs are far too small for sums of values → digit sums. S(23) + S(41) = 5 + 5 = 10 ✓; S(27) + S(45) = 9 + 9 = 18 ✓. So S(35) + S(26) = 8 + 8 = **16**. (61 is the plain sum.)
practice.shortcut: Two-digit inputs, small outputs → add all the digits.

practice.solution: Adding digit sums separately fails (11 + 9 = 20 ≠ 11). Add first, then sum the digits: 38 + 27 = 65 → 11 ✓; 54 + 18 = 72 → 9 ✓. So 46 + 37 = 83 → 8 + 3 = **11**. (20 is the separate digit-sum trap.)
practice.shortcut: Carries make S(a+b) differ from S(a)+S(b) — test both.

practice.solution: S(12) = 3, S(31) = 4 → 3 × 4 = 12 ✓; S(22) = 4, S(15) = 6 → 24 ✓. Rule: product of digit sums. So S(41) × S(23) = 5 × 5 = **25**. (10 adds the digit sums.)
practice.shortcut: Digit sums that multiply to the output → S(a) × S(b).

practice.solution: Reverse each input, then add: 21 + 32 = 53 ✓; 13 + 41 = 54 ✓. So 12 + 23 = **35**. (53 adds the unreversed inputs — which is exactly row 1's output, a planted trap.)
practice.shortcut: Outputs look like sums of flipped numbers → reverse first.

practice.solution: 25 + 17 = 42 → reversed 24 ✓; 38 + 16 = 54 → reversed 45 ✓. Rule: reverse the sum. So 19 + 33 = 52 → **25**. (52 forgets to reverse; 124 reverses the inputs instead: 91 + 33.)
practice.shortcut: Sum first, flip second.

practice.solution: Plain difference fails (52 − 13 = 39). Reverse the first number, then subtract: 25 − 13 = 12 ✓; 17 − 9 = 8 ✓. So 38 − 20 = **18**. (63 = 83 − 20 skips the reversal; 36 reverses the difference instead.)
practice.shortcut: Reverse only the two-digit input when the other is small.

practice.solution: 8 = 2 × 4 and 18 = 3 × 6 — multiply the digits. So 5 × 7 = **35**. (12 adds the digits.)
practice.shortcut: Output = digit product: check with the first pair.

practice.solution: Digit sums give 9, not 10, for row 1 — try digit products: 6 + 4 = 10 ✓; 6 + 10 = 16 ✓. So P(43) + P(62) = 12 + 12 = **24**. (15 adds digit sums; 144 multiplies the two products.)
practice.shortcut: Digit sums miss by a little → switch to digit products.

practice.solution: S(13) × 5 = 4 × 5 = 20 ✓; S(42) × 3 = 6 × 3 = 18 ✓. Rule: digit sum of the first × second. So 6 × 4 = **24**. (204 multiplies the raw values; 10 adds instead of multiplying.)
practice.shortcut: Small second input + two-digit first → shrink the first, keep the second.

practice.solution: S(25) = 7 → 2 × 7 + 4 = 18 ✓; S(31) = 4 → 2 × 4 + 6 = 14 ✓. Rule: twice the first number's digit sum plus the second. So 2 × 11 + 3 = **25**. (14 forgets to double; 22 forgets the + second.)
practice.shortcut: Output − second number is even and small → 2 × digit sum.
